content_voiceover: This dense but high-yield table shows how DOACs interfere with routine and specialty coagulation assays, split into direct thrombin inhibitors like dabigatran and direct factor Xa inhibitors like the xabans. Both classes prolong APTT and PT/INR, but thrombin inhibitors prolong thrombin clotting time, TCT, markedly while Xa inhibitors have no effect on TCT, this is actually a useful way to distinguish the two classes if you don't know which drug a patient is on. Clauss fibrinogen is generally unaffected, though thrombin inhibitors can factitiously lower it. Antithrombin activity assays are affected based on the substrate used, Xa-based AT assays are factitiously overestimated by Xa inhibitors, while thrombin-based AT assays are factitiously overestimated by thrombin inhibitors. Protein C and Protein S clot-based assays are factitiously overestimated by both drug classes, but chromogenic assays are unaffected, so chromogenic methods are preferred when a patient is on a DOAC. APTT-based factor assays and PT-based factor assays both show factitiously low results for multiple factors. Importantly, both drug classes cause incomplete correction on mixing studies, which can mimic a lupus anticoagulant or inhibitor, and both can cause lupus anticoagulant tests to be misclassified as positive. This is a classic board pitfall, a DOAC in the specimen can masquerade as an acquired inhibitor.
keypoints: TCT is markedly prolonged by thrombin inhibitors but unaffected by Xa inhibitors, a key differentiator
Chromogenic Protein C, Protein S, and antithrombin assays are more reliable than clot-based assays on DOACs
Both DOAC classes cause factitiously low clot-based factor assay results
DOACs cause incomplete mixing study correction and can mimic lupus anticoagulant
keypoint_voiceover: High-yield points for boards. Thrombin clotting time is markedly prolonged by thrombin inhibitors but unaffected by Xa inhibitors, a useful way to distinguish the two drug classes. Chromogenic assays for protein C, protein S, and antithrombin are more reliable than clot-based assays in patients on DOACs. Both drug classes cause factitiously low results on clot-based factor assays. And critically, DOACs can cause incomplete mixing study correction and falsely mimic a lupus anticoagulant.
